feed.subtitle: Research papers and global crypto regulation, at a glance
feed.rights: Explanations and summaries are generated by AI from the original text. Dates, rates and amounts are checked against the source, but errors are still possible, so always rely on the original. Nothing here is legal, tax or investment advice.

entry.title: Can Discrete Tokens Represent Images Without Semantic Loss? This paper tests whether quantizing visual signals into discrete tokens loses meaning, and proposes a new quantization method.
entry.summary: Can Discrete Tokens Serve as Semantically Lossless Representations of Visual Signals? arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 The paper challenges the assumption that quantization error inevitably causes semantic loss, finding that discrete representations with larger errors can sometimes understand better. The effective bit budget of discrete indices is identified as the key factor. The authors propose Factorized Vector Quantization, which uses symmetric parallel codebooks to quantize complementary views of visual features, continuing to improve at larger bit budgets. The model reaches state-of-the-art results among discrete-representation models and is competitive with continuous models such as Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained OCR. ★★★★ Notable: Challenges the assumption that quantization error inevitably loses semantics; factorized quantization matches continuous representations in multimodal understanding with large-scale comparisons.

entry.title: When to Intervene at Test Time: PORTAL, a Controller for Timing Interventions and Label Queries
entry.summary: When Should We Intervene at Test Time? arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper studies test-time adaptation, where a deployed model's intervention can help some input batches and hurt others. The authors propose PORTAL, a controller that decides when to deploy an intervention, which inputs to label, and when to stop querying labels. Experiments show that it turns an intervention that lowers overall accuracy into a useful choice on selected batches and prevents severe failures from changes in arrival order. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes a controller comparing candidate rules via shared labels with adaptive stopping; novel, with broad corruption-stream experiments, but impact stays mostly within test-time adaptation.

entry.title: Repulsive Landau Interactions Between Fermi Polarons at Strong Coupling
entry.summary: Mediated Interactions between Fermi Polarons in the Strongly Interacting Regime arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper studies mediated interactions between quasiparticles emerging from a Fermi sea, known as Fermi polarons, using zero-temperature quantum Monte Carlo methods. The main result is that the Landau interaction between polarons stays repulsive across all coupling strengths on the polaronic branch in the strongly interacting regime. The authors also compute the real-space interaction between static impurities, which shows RKKY-like behavior at weak coupling and matches the nonperturbative Born-Oppenheimer result at strong coupling. ★★★★ Notable: Zero-temperature quantum Monte Carlo reveals repulsive polaron-polaron interactions at strong coupling, contrasting experiments and recovering RKKY and Born-Oppenheimer limits.

entry.title: Classical verification of quantum computation beyond the polynomial hierarchy
entry.summary: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 The paper studies whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can check arbitrary quantum polynomial-time computations without computational assumptions. Relative to a classical oracle, it constructs a language outside the polynomial hierarchy that is exactly decidable in quantum polynomial time, with a public-coin protocol having perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4. The message count is shown to be optimal up to a constant factor. ★★★★ Notable: Constructs an oracle-relative language beyond the polynomial hierarchy with a perfectly complete public-coin proof system, using a new switching theorem for correlated restrictions; novel and rigorous

entry.title: Know, Then Draw: A New Training Approach for Visual Generation
entry.summary: Know, then Draw: A New Learning Paradigm for Visual Generation arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper proposes a learning paradigm that uses autoregressive pretraining to acquire semantic knowledge and diffusion post-training for high-fidelity rendering. Controlled comparisons find autoregression to be the stronger pretraining objective for downstream rendering, and it introduces a purely semantic tokenizer trained with language supervision alone. The authors establish compute-optimal scaling laws for both stages and train a 3B-parameter text-to-image model that scores 86 on GenEval and 87 on DPG-Bench. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes a knowledge-then-rendering paradigm, with controlled comparisons and scaling laws showing autoregressive pretraining beats diffusion from scratch.

entry.title: Timestral: A Family of Time Series Foundation Models for Probabilistic Forecasting
entry.summary: Timestral arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper introduces Timestral, four time series foundation models with 5M to 209M parameters for probabilistic forecasting. The authors report state-of-the-art results on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, with the 209M and 123M models taking the top two places on every metric. The approach combines Decoupled Horizon Forecasting, a covariate framework supporting known-future covariates in a causal architecture, and a two-stage pipeline of synthetic-data pretraining followed by post-training on mixed real and synthetic data with extended context. ★★★★ Notable: Introduces decoupled horizon forecasting and reports state-of-the-art results on three major benchmarks, giving solid evidence and moderate field impact.

entry.title: Minimum subpacketization of Reed-Solomon codes for cut-set-optimal linear repair
entry.summary: The Minimum Subpacketization of Reed-Solomon Codes with Linear Repair Achieving the Cut-Set Bound arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper studies the smallest subpacketization of Reed-Solomon codes that allow exact linear repair of every coordinate from any d helpers while meeting the cut-set bound. It proves a lower bound of sG_s(d+1) and shows it equals sG_s(n) when d(d+2) ≥ 4(n+1). The paper also gives a finite formula for G_s(n), an asymptotic growth result, and an affine-plane example showing sG_s(n) is not universal, along with a conjecture. ★★★★ Notable: Proves tight minimum subpacketization for RS codes under a degree condition, with proofs, impacting distributed storage coding theory.

entry.title: Following Gradients to Find Training Data That Erodes Model Safety
entry.summary: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 The paper shows that fine-tuning large language models on instruction data can weaken their safety even when individual examples look harmless. It introduces SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies training examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. Using it, the authors build SafeTulu by removing the 20% of Tulu 3 examples most aligned with unsafe responses, which reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo while largely preserving capability. ★★★★ Notable: Simplifies low-rank gradient attribution to scale to million-example filtering, cutting GCG attack success up to 22% across several models.

entry.title: Concordat: a Python library that enforces step-by-step rules on LLM agents at run time
entry.summary: Concordat: Typed Sessions for LLM Agents arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 Concordat is an open-source Python library that models an LLM agent's allowed behaviour as a finite-state protocol enforced during execution. On each turn the model sees only the tools legal in its current state, and illegal calls are rejected before side effects occur. In an evaluation on 50 tau-bench airline tasks with simulated customers pressing for skipped confirmations, the standard agent made unconfirmed changes in several tasks while the Concordat agent made none, with no significant difference in task success. ★★★★ Notable: Applies session types and typestate to enforce protocols on LLM agents at runtime, a novel approach; evaluation is limited to tau-bench airline tasks.

entry.title: M4Bench: A Benchmark for Procedural Specs in EHR Derivation Agents
entry.summary: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper introduces M4Bench, a benchmark of 28 clinical variable derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU. It tests whether AI coding agents can reproduce these derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills affect their results. Skills raised reward by 0.136 on average, mostly due to specification completeness, while only a few runs passed every strict check. The tasks, skills, evaluation code, and run evidence are released as open source. ★★★★ Notable: Introduces a new clinical derivation benchmark and decomposes skill value through multiple controlled experiments, offering useful insight for the subfield.

entry.title: SecDMP: A Provably Secure Data Prefetcher Defense (Extended Version)
entry.summary: SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching (Extended Version) arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 Data memory-dependent prefetchers (DMPs) are a CPU optimization in recent mainstream processors that can improve performance but may leak secrets through side channels. The paper classifies DMP leakage, categorizes existing and new attacks, and validates the analysis by implementing open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor. It proposes SecDMP, a hardware defense in which secrets are marked in memory so DMPs never encode them in the microarchitecture. The authors formally prove SecDMP adds no leakage beyond a baseline without DMPs. ★★★★★ Notable: Classifies DMP leakage and proposes SecDMP, a formally proven hardware defense blocking all leakage classes while preserving public-data performance.

entry.title: FeatureArc: Testing Coding Agents on Features That Grow Over Time
entry.summary: FeatureArc: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Evolving Features arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper introduces FeatureArc, a benchmark that evaluates coding agents on software features that evolve through successive stages, with each extension building on the agent's own earlier code. Tasks are built from repository histories and checked with executable tests across four programming languages. Evaluating 10 agents on 73 tasks, pooled success falls from 62.7% at the first stage to 28.5% on the whole feature. Inherited defects from earlier stages are a common cause of failure. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes a benchmark and pipeline for evolving features; experiments on 10 agents and 73 tasks reveal a large first-stage versus whole-feature success gap.

entry.title: Shared Latent Number Geometry Across Text and Image Arithmetic
entry.summary: Beyond the Readout: A Latent Numerical Frame Shared Across Modality and Operation arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper asks whether a multimodal model uses one internal concept of number for arithmetic given as text or as an image. Using causal interventions on Gemma4-12B-it's residual stream, the authors learn subspaces where swapping coordinates changes the model's answer. The subspaces for different conditions use different directions but can be aligned by one rotation and rescaling. The study also finds hidden directions that carry the number without affecting the current output digit and that steer later digits. ★★★★ Notable: Uses causal interventions rather than similarity metrics to show text and image arithmetic share one numerical geometry, with hidden directions carrying the number.

entry.title: LinMix: Data Mixing Framed as Linear Domain Attribution
entry.summary: LinMix: Data Mixing as Linear Domain Attribution arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper studies how the mixture of domains in a language model's pretraining data affects performance. It proposes LinMix, which samples data mixes at the vertices of a capped simplex so each domain is at its cap or absent, yielding an interpretable linear model whose coefficients are domain attributions. In pretraining experiments with 1B and 4B parameter models, LinMix outperforms Dirichlet-based mixing on reasoning, code, and math benchmarks, and it supports linear fitting across 288 fine-grained domains. ★★★★ Notable: Recasts data mixing as linear domain attribution, replacing Dirichlet with vertex sampling and proving optimality; evaluated on two models and several benchmarks, giving fairly solid evidence.

entry.title: TRIDENT-Seq: Label-Efficient Payment Risk Modeling via Profile-Matched Prefix-Future Contrast
entry.summary: TRIDENT-Seq: Profile-Matched Prefix-Future Contrast for Label-Efficient Payment Risk Modeling arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper presents TRIDENT-Seq, a transaction foundation model pretrained on unlabeled payment histories using Prefix-Future Contrast (PFC), which matches each prefix to summaries of subsequent behavior among candidates with similar activity profiles. Across three production payment businesses, the pretrained encoder improves average precision and recall at a 0.5% intervention budget over scratch training with the same architecture. In a deployment evaluation at Ant International, recorded amount-based chargeback and overall loss rates are 37.7% and 37.9% lower than those of the previous XGBoost-based system. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes profile-matched prefix-future contrast beating random candidates; validated across three production businesses with label efficiency gains and deployment loss reductions.

entry.title: Measurement incompatibility and noiseless quantum codes: a theory paper on whether quantum channels can preserve measurement incompatibility
entry.summary: Measurement incompatibility and noiseless quantum codes arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper studies when a quantum channel universally preserves the incompatibility of measurements. The authors construct a rank-one minimal informationally complete measurement and prove that such preservation holds if and only if the input space contains a noiseless code subspace of full output dimension. They also give an explicit construction of exact encodings and connect the results to quantum steering and quantum error correction. ★★★★ Notable: Constructs a rank-one MIC and proves equivalence with noiseless codes, resolving a conjecture with thorough proofs; impact mainly within quantum information theory.

entry.title: Quantum key distribution secured by a bound on information leakage
entry.summary: Prepare-and-measure quantum key distribution from a bound on information leakage arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper examines whether, in prepare-and-measure quantum key distribution, a single bound on information leakage from the sender's source can replace a detailed model of the source. The authors show that this bound, quantified by the probability of guessing the input from everything the source emits, suffices to prove security against collective attacks, with no assumptions on the form, dimension, energy or purity of the emitted states. They note that the standard B92 and BB84 protocols cannot certify a key under this assumption, whereas closely related protocols can reach one secret bit per round in the ideal limit. For noisy implementations, key rates are computed with semidefinite programming relaxations, and the best protocols tolerate visibilities down to 0.84, corresponding to an 8% quantum bit error rate, versus the 11% threshold of device-dependent BB84. ★★★★ Notable: Proves security from a single leakage bound without device modeling, reaching near-ideal key rates; validation rests mainly on theory and SDP computations.

entry.title: Low-degree polynomial lower bounds for clustering in low dimensions
entry.summary: Low-degree polynomials lower bounds for clustering in small dimension arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper studies the computational limits of clustering n observations from a mixture of K isotropic distributions in R^d when K is much larger than d. It constructs a mixture of Bernoulli product distributions whose centers come from a dual BCH code, so that moment tensors match those of the uniform distribution up to a given order. For suitable separations, low-degree polynomials require roughly K^2 d^{3/2} observations, and via Gaussianization the hardness extends to isotropic Gaussian mixtures. ★★★★ Notable: Using dual BCH codes and bipartite-graph polynomial families, it improves the low-degree lower bound from dK² to K²d^{3/2} with proof.

entry.title: Watermark Basins: Detecting Distilled LLMs Using Only API Access
entry.summary: Watermark Basins: Black-Box Detection of Distilled LLMs arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper addresses API-based distillation, where an adversary trains a student model on a proprietary teacher model's outputs, and how providers can watermark outputs to detect it. The authors find that watermarked training creates a persistent, key-specific geometric signal in parameter space, orthogonal to ordinary fine-tuning directions. They propose WM-Basin, a black-box detector that needs only API queries, and report that it outperforms a token-level baseline on mathematical reasoning distillation while the signal survives quantization, pruning, and reinforcement-learning post-training. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes a watermark basin signal orthogonal to task subspaces, detected via gradient alignment; evaluated across 135M to 8.2B students with clear gains over the token-level baseline.

entry.title: Your Policy Is Secretly a Harness: How Agent Interfaces Shape Decisions
entry.summary: Your Policy Is Secretly a Harness: The Decision Geometry of Agent Interfaces arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper studies how language model agents depend on their harness, the prompts, tools, and control logic that present tasks to the model. Under KL-regularized control, the authors show that a trained policy's log odds reflect its harness's action preferences, and that deployed return equals the harness ceiling minus the policy's mismatch. In MiniWoB++, reversing observation field order drops a trained model's success from 85.0% to 19.2%. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes a theory that policy log odds encode harness preferences under KL control, validated on MiniWoB++ and Terminal-Bench with clear empirical effects.

entry.title: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs and the Trust Trap in Graph Learning
entry.summary: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs, Exposure, and the Trust Trap in Multi-Relational Graph Learning arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper studies multi-relational graph detectors, which learn how much to trust each relation from clean data, while attackers face different manipulation costs per relation. It proves that degree gating beats any selection or reweighting of a relation when part of the population is isolated on it and the attacker cannot afford to open the gate. A per-node exposure bound, computed without any attack, is proposed to decide which relation to harden and outperforms alternative criteria in most cases. Without cost information, the authors conclude the safe choice is to abstain from using the graph. ★★★★ Notable: Proves degree gating strictly beats relation selection under sharp conditions, with real-graph validation and exact worst-case bounds; impact is confined to graph-security subfield.

entry.title: Do Generalist Skill Optimizers Really Help AI Agents? A Bipartite Attribution Rethink
entry.summary: Does Your Generalist Skill Optimizer Really Incentivize Agentic Tasks? Rethinking Skill Optimization via Bipartite Attribution arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper introduces BiPA, a method for evaluating skill optimizers that rewrite an AI agent's natural-language procedures to improve performance on long-horizon tasks. Across three optimizers, three benchmarks, and two models, learned skills succeed about as often as their hand-written seeds, and development-set gains vanish on the test set. The optimized skills also increase input tokens by about 16%, largely because the added rules cause extra conversation turns. The authors propose four principles, including accepting only edits whose gains exceed what selection alone would report. ★★★★ Notable: Introduces bipartite attribution and selection baselines showing dev-set gains vanish on test and inputs grow about 16%, with multi-benchmark, multi-model experiments.

entry.title: PipeLink: Contract-Guided Linking of GPU Kernel Components
entry.summary: PipeLink: Contract-Guided Linking of GPU Kernel Components arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents PipeLink, a linker that combines separately compiled GPU kernel components using contracts stating what each component requires and provides. PipeLink checks these contracts, solves a joint placement of streaming multiprocessor resources, and generates the transfers between components. Across 51 configurations on Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, linked kernels run within 0.2% of the same sources compiled as one unit. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes a contract-guided linker for GPU kernel components; validated across 51 configurations within 0.2% of monolithic builds, with practical composition speedups.

entry.title: WorkFactory: Converting Professional Intents into Executable Tasks to Scale Agent Training
entry.summary: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper presents WorkFactory, a framework that builds an information support graph from professional intents and uses probe executions to find and repair missing task information. It constructs 112,686 tasks across 612 occupations and fine-tunes Qwen models on the resulting teacher trajectories, producing the WorkPilot family. The authors report that all three models improve over their base models on four professional-work benchmarks. ★★★★ Notable: Information support graph and probe-based repair for constructing professional tasks offers substantive improvement; multi-benchmark, multi-scale experiments with ablations give solid evidence, with m

entry.title: MixSIS: Instance segmentation that mixes annotation types
entry.summary: MixSIS: Mixed-supervised instance segmentation arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper proposes Mixed-Supervised Instance Segmentation (MixSIS), a task where a dataset can combine image, point, box, and mask annotations. The authors introduce AnnotationsMixer (AnnsMixer) as a baseline that generates pseudo mask annotations from all these annotation levels, even within a single image. The paper reports that AnnsMixer largely outperforms state-of-the-art methods on weakly-supervised and MixSIS tasks, and shows in three case studies how it can reduce annotation time or improve results. ★★★★ Notable: Introduces a new mixed-annotation instance segmentation task and baseline, largely outperforming prior methods on WSIS and MixSIS with three supporting case studies.

entry.title: Matrix samplers and quantum-proof extractors: equivalence and near-optimal constructions
entry.summary: Matrix Samplers and Quantum-Proof Extractors: Their Correspondence and Almost-Optimal Constructions arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper establishes an equivalence between matrix samplers and quantum-proof randomness extractors, extending Zuckerman's classical sampler-extractor correspondence. Using this equivalence, the authors construct explicit strong matrix samplers with optimal randomness overhead and near-optimal sample complexity. They also obtain strong quantum-proof extractors with improved seed and output lengths. ★★★★ Notable: Establishes equivalence between matrix samplers and quantum-proof extractors, improving sample complexity and seed length over prior matrix samplers.

entry.title: Blindfold: Keeping Random Audit Checks Hidden from LLM Agents
entry.summary: Blindfold: Keeping the Audit Coin Secret from LLM Agents arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies audit-based certification, which limits an LLM agent's violation rate by auditing a random fraction of its actions and reweighting the results. The authors show that validity also requires the audit coin to stay hidden from the agent before its action is committed. They define this as pre-commit noninterference, measure it, and derive bounds on the resulting bias. Experiments on a monitor and a real LLM agent show that a visible audit notice leaks the coin and breaks the certificate, while a silent audit or a fresh coin per audited call restores validity. ★★★★ Notable: Introduces pre-commit noninterference with tight bias bounds, a novel theory; experiments on LLM agents confirm the channel but at limited scale.

entry.title: V-LUMEN: Visual Lookup Memory for Scaling Embeddings in Vision-Language Models
entry.summary: V-LUMEN: Visual Lookup Memory for Embedding Scaling in Vision-Language Models arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper introduces V-LUMEN, a visual lookup memory for vision-language models that adds external memory instead of increasing model size. It discretizes visual features with a frozen codebook, builds spatially aware memory keys by hashing, modulates them with text-conditioned relevance signals, and fuses retrieved embeddings into the backbone through a gated residual pathway. On five reasoning-intensive benchmarks it improves a frozen Qwen3-VL-2B backbone and transfers zero-shot to three benchmarks whose images are disjoint from the training data. ★★★★ Notable: Applies lookup-based external memory to VLMs with spatial hashing and gated fusion, validated on five benchmarks with moderate experimental scope.

entry.title: The State of Multilingual LLM Evaluation: An Audit of 51 Benchmarks
entry.summary: The State and Fate of Multilingual, Contextual Evaluation in the NLP World arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper audits 51 recent multilingual benchmarks covering 242 datasets and 219 languages, examining coverage, representativeness, and rigor. It finds that many languages appear in only one benchmark, low-resource languages are evaluated on far fewer task categories, and 56% of dataset-language instances are translated from English. The authors also report benchmark contamination. They conclude with recommendations for natively constructed, culturally grounded, contamination-aware evaluation frameworks. ★★★★ Notable: A data-driven audit of 51 multilingual benchmarks across coverage, representativeness, and rigor offers a fresh, well-evidenced critique.

entry.title: PailitaoMMSearch2.0 Technical Report: Scaling Generative Retrieval to Unified End-to-End Multimodal Search
entry.summary: PailitaoMMSearch2.0 Technical Report: Scaling Generative Retrieval to Unified End-to-End Multimodal Search arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents PailitaoMMSearch, a system that generates product Semantic IDs directly from a raw query image and free-form instruction, aiming for unified end-to-end multimodal search. It scales along data, intent, and scenario dimensions, using continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. The system is deployed in Taobao Pailitao, and a controlled online A/B test reports statistically significant gains in item page views, transactions, and gross merchandise value. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes a unified end-to-end multimodal generative retrieval system with CPT and RL; a controlled Taobao A/B test shows significant gains, indicating broad impact.

entry.title: DocXEval: A Systematic Evaluation of Explainability in Multimodal Document Understanding
entry.summary: DocXEval: A Systematic Evaluation of Explainability in Multimodal Document Understanding arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper introduces DocXEval, a comprehensive explainability framework for multimodal document understanding that combines text, layout, and image. It adapts existing explainable AI methods and metrics to this setting and adds multi-target variants for tasks such as semantic entity recognition. The authors evaluate 13 XAI methods across 3 tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 metrics, finding that Occlusion is the most faithful and interpretable overall. The work also includes a meta-evaluation of metrics and dataset-wide analyses of model behavior. ★★★★ Notable: First XAI framework for multimodal document understanding, systematically evaluating 13 methods and 17 metrics across 8 datasets and 4 models, with solid evidence.

entry.title: Can Lightweight Decision Models Classify Why Retrieved Sources Conflict in RAG?
entry.summary: Do We Need an LLM to Know Why Sources Conflict? Decision Models for Knowledge-Conflict Typing in RAG arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 When retrieved sources disagree, the appropriate response depends on the type of conflict. This paper tests whether decision models, which output probabilities over fixed options in a single forward pass, can classify conflict types quickly and cheaply. On the CONFLICTS benchmark, 10 of 11 decision models match or exceed Gemini 2.5 Flash (61.3%) in accuracy, at 4 to 39 times lower billed cost. ★★★★ Notable: Applies decision models to RAG conflict typing, comparing against LLMs and cascades on a benchmark with extensive experiments; useful for the subfield.

entry.title: GUI-JEPA: A Fast, Decoder-Free Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents Using JEPA Latents
entry.summary: GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper introduces GUI-JEPA, a decoder-free action policy for mobile GUI agents built on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture. It selects actions in the latent space of an encoder pretrained on unlabelled GUI screenshots, using an action- and region-conditioned predictor to score all candidate actions in one batched pass. On AndroidControl, it is reported to run 2.8-4.0x faster than a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B agent, using 6% of its parameters while reaching 86-92% of its in-distribution accuracy. ★★★★ Notable: A novel decoder-free JEPA latent policy for GUI agents; AndroidControl results show speed and parameter gains over a 7B baseline, but accuracy remains below it.

entry.title: Switchable unlearning that removes training data while keeping retrieval ability.
entry.summary: Forget the Data, Keep the Capability: Switchable Unlearning for Retrieval arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper presents MoME, a framework that lets one model switch between Full mode for standard inference and Core mode for unlearned inference, supporting privacy requests to delete individuals' training data. Core parameters receive no gradients from the forget set, making Core independent of that data, and the authors introduce the Forgetting-Rank statistic to audit this independence. On Market-1501, VeRi-776, and RegDB, Core performs near a retrained reference under three membership attacks while retrieving above it. ★★★★ Notable: Gradient-isolated switchable branches enable unlearning, audited by a rank statistic; validated across three datasets and several backbones.

entry.title: Evolving Agent Teams: A Multi-Agent Framework Escaping Local Optima
entry.summary: Evolving Agent Teams arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper finds that existing coding agents converge to local optima when optimizing real-world expert-written GPU kernels such as FlashInfer. The authors propose Evolving Agent Teams, in which a central supervisor diagnoses local optima and restructures the agent team, while a persistent file system stores accumulated experience. With an extended token budget, the generated CUDA kernel reaches a 1.2x mean speedup over the production FlashInfer MLA paged decode kernel and wins on 36 of 47 FlashInfer-Bench workloads. ★★★★ Notable: A supervisor restructures agent teams using persistent memory, with large speedups on several real kernel and robotics tasks.

entry.title: Right Click, Wrong Box: Judging GUI Clicks by Their Outcomes
entry.summary: Right Click, Wrong Box: Grading GUI Grounding by What a Click Does arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper argues that GUI grounding benchmarks count a click as correct only inside one annotated box, even though interfaces often expose the same action through several elements. The authors define a click as correct when it produces the same outcome as the annotated target, and build outcome maps and an execution judge by executing about a thousand clicks per page on live web applications. Testing three strong grounders on a code forge and an online shop, they find that many box-rejected clicks still reach the intended outcome, and an audit on ScreenSpot-v2 yields corrections of 0.2 to 1.8 points. ★★★★★ Notable: Proposes outcome-based grading of GUI clicks, validated via live execution probes and a blind audit on ScreenSpot-v2.

entry.title: HqcLethe: streaming HQC key encapsulation for tiny stateless servers
entry.summary: HqcLethe: Streaming HQC Encapsulation for Tiny Stateless Servers arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents HqcLethe, a stateless post-quantum key exchange that streams an HQC key encapsulation in packet-sized pieces, so servers need not buffer multi-packet handshakes and avoid memory-exhaustion attacks. It uses the Chinese remainder theorem to split polynomial multiplication into independent, masked remainders, one per packet. The authors prove in Rocq with SSProve that the masked pieces reveal no more than an ordinary HQC ciphertext, and verify session secrecy, server authentication and forward secrecy in ProVerif. On a Raspberry Pi 3B+, each worker uses a fixed 1.2-1.6 MiB, and at category 5 it sends 27x fewer bytes and uses 9.0x less server CPU than McTiny. ★★★★ Notable: Uses the Chinese remainder theorem to split HQC polynomial multiplication into independent packet pieces, with formal proofs and protocol verification.

entry.title: Language Models Keep Abandoned Analyses: Residue and Adaptation after Garden-Path Sentences
entry.summary: Language Models Keep Abandoned Analyses: Residue and Adaptation after Garden-Path Sentences arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper examines whether language models keep using syntactic analyses they have abandoned after reading garden-path sentences. Across 24 open models, the authors find a residue of the abandoned analysis that raises later object attachment, plus an adaptation toward the resolved structure. Activation patching shows the residue is carried by noun-phrase states computed before disambiguation, and replacing them removes most of it in the larger models. ★★★★ Notable: Activation patching separates residue from adaptation across 24 models, a novel mechanistic framing with broad, controlled experimental support.

entry.title: Does LLM pre-training usually happen at the edge of stability?
entry.summary: Does LLM Pre-Training Typically Occur at the Edge of Stability? arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper revisits how well quadratic approximations model neural network training, especially in large language model (LLM) pretraining. It identifies an "Edge of Convexity" (EoC) failure mode, where persistent negative curvature makes the quadratic dynamics diverge regardless of learning rate, and proposes a generalized Edge of Stability (EoS) definition for stochastic adaptive optimizers. Across LLM pretraining runs with models up to 787M parameters, EoC is always observed, while EoS is common but not universal, disappearing at sufficiently small learning rates or batch sizes below a critical threshold. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes Edge of Convexity and generalizes Edge of Stability, validated systematically across LLM pretraining runs up to 787M parameters.

entry.title: Learning to correct interpolation for reconstructing intermediate scientific fields
entry.summary: Generative Refinement Learning for Temporal Interpolation in Scientific Machine Learning arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper proposes iFLEX, a method for reconstructing unobserved intermediate scientific fields between two observation times. It first forms a time-weighted average of the two observations, then uses a conditional diffusion model to learn and generate the residual between this average and the true intermediate field. The authors evaluate it on Navier-Stokes Kraichnan turbulence, Shanghai radar precipitation, and sea surface temperature data, reporting lower reconstruction error than the compared baselines. ★★★★ Notable: Learns residuals over weighted averaging with a conditional diffusion model, benchmarked on three scientific datasets against optical-flow and video baselines; useful for the subfield.

entry.title: Nonlinear Direct Feedback Alignment: a scalable training method without backpropagation
entry.summary: Nonlinear Direct Feedback Alignment for Scalable Backpropagation-Free Training arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper addresses the biological implausibility and backward locking of backpropagation by improving Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA). The proposed Nonlinear Direct Feedback Alignment (NDFA) builds each hidden-layer feedback path with a lightweight nonlinear surrogate subnetwork, which is updated by a dedicated learning strategy. Experiments on residual networks and vision transformers across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and ImageNet show that NDFA outperforms existing DFA-based methods and narrows the gap to backpropagation. ★★★★ Notable: Replaces fixed DFA feedback matrices with a learned nonlinear surrogate subnetwork; broad experiments on several datasets and architectures narrow the gap to BP.

entry.title: Conservative Dueling Bandits: Learning Preferences While Staying Near a Trusted Baseline
entry.summary: Conservative Dueling Bandits: Preference Learning under Baseline Constraints arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies conservative contextual dueling bandits, which learn from pairwise comparisons while requiring that the displayed better option's cumulative score stay above a fraction of a trusted baseline's. The authors show that directly transferring CLUCB's safety test can incur linear regret. They propose MaxInP-BC for linear utilities and BTIGW-BC for general utility classes. Both algorithms satisfy the constraint with high probability at all times, with regret bounds that include a cost of conservatism. ★★★★ Notable: Introduces a new safety constraint for dueling bandits, shows CLUCB's test fails with linear regret, and gives two algorithms with guarantees validated experimentally.

entry.title: Looking at the Image Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Faster Diffusion VLMs
entry.summary: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 Diffusion vision-language models process the full input at every denoising step, and visual tokens make up 89-97% of that input on the studied benchmarks. The authors propose LOWN, a decoding method that first predicts masked tokens without the image and processes the image only when this disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Agreement lets earlier predictions be reused, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked at each step. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score across ten benchmarks while using 35.3% of decoding FLOPs on average. ★★★★ Notable: Certificate-guided adaptive image routing is moderately novel; ten-benchmark results retaining 99.6% score at 35.3% FLOPs give solid evidence, with impact limited to diffusion VLMs.

entry.title: Shows that all bidders in repeated auctions cannot jointly achieve no-regret learning under budget constraints.
entry.summary: Impossibility of No-Regret in Multi-Agent Bidding arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper studies repeated second-price auctions with multiple pacing bidders facing budget or return-on-investment constraints. It proves that it is computationally impossible for all bidders to achieve no-regret simultaneously, linking high variance in bidding systems to high regret. The authors show joint no-regret is PPAD-hard by extracting a pacing equilibrium from low-variance systems. Simulations suggest that several widely used bidding algorithms can cycle and display high-variance behavior even in simple markets. ★★★★★ Notable: Proves joint no-regret in multi-agent bidding is PPAD-hard via a variance-regret link, a novel and consequential impossibility result.

entry.title: Tight limits on fair AMM mechanism design under weak efficiency
entry.summary: Tight Characterizations of AMM Mechanism Design under Weak Efficiency arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies miner extractable value (MEV) in automated market makers (AMMs), where block builders can profit by controlling transaction order. It proves that no deterministic, anonymous batch AMM can be both incentive compatible and weakly locally efficient under plain consensus without fair sequencing, even with censorship resilience and unlimited block space. The impossibility relies on Sybil identities, over-reporting budgets, and misreporting values. Removing any one of these strategic capabilities makes both properties achievable under censorship resilience. ★★★★★ Notable: Proves impossibility of IC and wLE for deterministic anonymous batch AMMs under plain consensus, with tight characterization of strategy restrictions.

entry.title: Sybil-proof adaptive clinching auctions and their use in blockchain market design
entry.summary: Sybil-Proofness of Generalized Adaptive Clinching and Implications for Blockchain Mechanism Design arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper examines whether the adaptive clinching auction for budget-constrained bidders stays robust when a bidder splits its budget across fake identities. The authors propose a generalized adaptive clinching framework and prove that bidders gain nothing by splitting into any number of identities, as long as their total reported budget does not exceed their enforceable true budget. They extend the mechanism to a two-sided automated market maker for decentralized finance and show, through impossibility results, that these guarantees are essentially the best possible. ★★★★ Notable: Proves Sybil-robust incentive compatibility for adaptive clinching and designs a two-sided AMM, backed by impossibility results and proofs with broad DeFi relevance.

entry.title: Noise Shapes the Surplus: Strategic Play Against No-Regret Learners
entry.summary: Noise Shapes the Surplus: Strategic Play Against No-Regret Learners arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies how an optimizer in zero-sum games can gain cumulative payoff above the minimax benchmark against no-regret learners, here Follow-the-Regularized-Leader algorithms, that act on noisy payoff scores with decaying learning rates. Passive play earns at most constant surplus, while a clairvoyant optimizer secures surplus scaling with the inverse learning rate when the mean response is profitable. Active alternating play can still extract surplus from the learner's movement when it is not, and at the canonical rate the noiseless Ω(√T) surplus is recovered under mean-zero, finite-variance perturbations. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes new exploitation mechanisms against noisy FTRL learners, proving sqrt(T) surplus under decaying rates; strong theory, but scope is limited to zero-sum games.

entry.title: Balanced Subspace Compression for Mamba-2 Recurrent States
entry.summary: Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2 State Compression arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper proposes a post-training method that compresses the fixed-size recurrent state of Mamba-2 models by balanced truncation over the subspace that writes and reads the output, rather than scoring individual coordinates. It also introduces HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers. With HARP, halving the state dimension raises average WikiText-2 perplexity by 0.3 points (1.8%) across 130M to 2.7B models, compared with 1.6 points (9.3%) for GHOST. ★★★★ Notable: Applies balanced truncation to Mamba-2 state compression with layer-wise ranks from Hankel spectra, halving state dimension with 0.3 perplexity increase across 130M–2.7B.

entry.title: InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Build AI Infrastructure, and How to Judge Them
entry.summary: InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Develop AI Infrastructure, and How Can We Tell? arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper introduces InfraDev, a benchmark of 36 tasks drawn from real pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl, covering training, inference, and reinforcement learning infrastructure. Grading combines hidden probes that check requirements the original tests miss with a prompt that specifies the required interfaces. Across six frontier models, the best resolved 38.9% of the tasks, and the probes rejected 32% of submissions that passed all official tests. ★★★★ Notable: Builds a multi-file, multi-GPU infrastructure benchmark from real PRs with hidden probes, evaluated across six frontier models with failure analysis.

entry.title: Learning from Points and Patches: A Pre-trained Transformer for Time Series Analysis
entry.summary: Learning from Points and Patches: A Pre-trained Hybrid Attention Transformer for Time Series Analysis arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents TimeHAT, a general-purpose pre-training framework for time-series analysis. It introduces a unified point-patch masking strategy that combines point-level and patch-level supervision for contextual reconstruction and causal extrapolation, along with a hybrid attention encoder intended to preserve contextual interactions while mitigating rank degeneration. The model is evaluated on real-world datasets across classification, long-term forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection, under fine-tuning, few-shot, and zero-shot settings, with competitive results reported. ★★★★ Notable: Combines unified point-patch masking with hybrid attention for time-series pre-training, validated across four downstream tasks and multiple transfer settings.
